recommendations.text: Avoid Open System Authentication. Use WPA2-Enterprise or WPA3 with 802.1X authentication to ensure only verified devices can connect.
recommendations.verbatimEvidence: Open system authentication is a null authentication algorithm that involves a two-step authentication transaction.
recommendations.technicalMeaning: Open authentication does not verify identity, allowing rogue AP impersonation.

recommendations.text: Implement strong authentication mechanisms. Use 802.1X/EAP to validate device identity and prevent unauthorized access.
recommendations.verbatimEvidence: Authentication mechanisms should ensure that devices connecting to the WLAN are properly validated.
recommendations.technicalMeaning: Weak authentication allows spoofed identities to access the network.

recommendations.text: Use modern encryption standards. Configure WPA2-AES or WPA3 and avoid deprecated protocols such as WEP and TKIP.
recommendations.verbatimEvidence: Early IEEE 802.11 security mechanisms had significant cryptographic weaknesses that could allow attackers to compromise confidentiality and integrity.
recommendations.technicalMeaning: Weak encryption enables interception and manipulation of data.

recommendations.text: Strengthen WLAN encryption policies. Enforce AES-based encryption and secure key management practices.
recommendations.verbatimEvidence: Organizations should use strong cryptographic protections to secure wireless communications.
recommendations.technicalMeaning: Strong cryptography protects against exploitation of weak security controls.

recommendations.text: Disable Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS). Turn off WPS to prevent brute-force PIN attacks and unauthorized access.
recommendations.verbatimEvidence: Organizations should configure wireless access points securely and disable unnecessary services.

recommendations.text: Harden access point configurations. Disable unused features like WPS and restrict unnecessary services.
recommendations.verbatimEvidence: Wireless networks should be securely configured and unnecessary features should be disabled.

recommendations.text: Enable Protected Management Frames (PMF). Use IEEE 802.11w to prevent spoofed deauthentication attacks.
recommendations.verbatimEvidence: Management frames in IEEE 802.11 networks were originally not protected, allowing attackers to forge management frames such as deauthentication and disassociation frames.
recommendations.technicalMeaning: Attackers can spoof deauthentication frames to disconnect users.

recommendations.text: Protect wireless management frames. Ensure management frame protection is enabled.
recommendations.verbatimEvidence: Unprotected management frames can be exploited by attackers to disrupt wireless communications.
recommendations.technicalMeaning: Lack of protection enables service disruption.

recommendations.text: Deploy WLAN protections against rogue activity. Enable PMF and monitor for unauthorized access points.
recommendations.verbatimEvidence: Security mechanisms should be implemented to prevent unauthorized access points and malicious wireless activity.
recommendations.technicalMeaning: PMF helps prevent rogue interference and control manipulation.
